title: Venn Diagrams
tagline: Year 2 — Set relationships and the inclusion-exclusion rule for two and three sets

introduction.overview: A Venn diagram uses overlapping circles to show how groups relate. Two kinds of question are asked. In the first, you choose the diagram that correctly represents the relation between given classes (cats and animals, doctors and women). In the second, you use numbers: how many belong to only one group, to both, or to neither. The counting problems are solved with the inclusion-exclusion rule.
introduction.placementRelevance: Venn diagram questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds, in both the diagram-choice form and the counting form.
introduction.realWorldContext: Survey analysis, overlapping customer segments and database queries (AND, OR, NOT) all use set logic.

learningObjectives: Choose the right Venn diagram for the relation between classes
Use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
Find "only", "exactly two", "at least two" and "none" regions
Fill a diagram from the centre outwards

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Union = everything in A or B (or both). Intersection = in both. Complement = in none of them. The total of all regions equals the size of the universe.

coreDefinitions: Set: a collection of objects. Universe U: the set of all objects under discussion.
Union A ∪ B: elements in A or B or both. Intersection A ∩ B: elements in both.
Only A = A − (A ∩ B). Neither = U − (A ∪ B).
Subset: if every Cat is an Animal, Cats form a circle inside Animals.
Disjoint sets: have no common elements; their circles do not overlap.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: When you add two groups, anyone in both is counted twice, so subtract the overlap once. With three groups, subtracting the three pairwise overlaps removes the triple overlap one time too many, so add it back once.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: For counting, start with the innermost region (all three), then fill the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair, then the "only one" regions by subtracting everything else.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Two sets
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Three sets
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣA − ΣAB + ABC
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Exactly two
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Pairs include the triple three times.

mainNarrative: To choose a diagram, think about class membership. Cats and Dogs are different classes, both inside Animals: two separate circles inside a bigger one. Women and Mothers: Mothers lie inside Women. If two classes can share members without one containing the other (Doctors and Women), draw two overlapping circles.
For two sets, use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). In a class of 40, with 25 liking tea, 20 coffee and 10 both, the number liking at least one is 35 and the number liking neither is 5.

For three sets, fill the diagram from the centre. With the data A = 45, B = 40, C = 30, AB = 15, BC = 10, AC = 8 and ABC = 5, the total in at least one is 45 + 40 + 30 − 15 − 10 − 8 + 5 = 87, so 13 play none.
To count regions: only A = A − AB − AC + ABC = 27; exactly two = AB + BC + AC − 3 × ABC = 18; at least two = exactly two + all three = 23.
Always check that all regions plus "none" add up to the total. This check catches most arithmetic slips.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why add back the triple
deepDiveAspects.content: People in all three sets are counted three times by the singles and subtracted three times by the pairs, so they vanish; adding ABC once restores them.

deepDiveAspects.title: Diagram-choice questions
deepDiveAspects.content: Look for classes that cannot overlap (cats and dogs), classes that are inside another (cats and animals), and classes that can partly overlap (doctors and women).

problemVariations.typeName: Exactly two or at least two

solvedExamples.title: Two sets
solvedExamples.question: In a class of 40, 25 like tea, 20 like coffee and 10 like both. How many like neither?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Those in both are counted once.

solvedExamples.title: Three sets
solvedExamples.question: In the survey of 100 students (cricket 45, football 40, hockey 30, A∩B 15, B∩C 10, A∩C 8, all three 5), how many play none of the three?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The triple overlap is added back once.

solvedExamples.title: Exactly two
solvedExamples.question: In the same survey, how many play exactly two of the three sports?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Remove the triple from each pair.

steps.title: Pairs only
steps.explanation: AB only = 10, BC only = 5, AC only = 3.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Each pair count includes the 5 who play all three.

shortcutMethods.title: Centre-out filling

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Fill the triple overlap first, then each pair minus the triple, then each single minus the rest. Total check at the end.

rulesForApplication: Only A = A − AB − AC + ABC.
Draw overlapping circles for partly overlapping classes.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Total must equal the sum of all regions; test options.

quickFormulas: A + B + C − AB − BC − AC + ABC

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find "neither" in a two-set problem?
Can I find "exactly two" in a three-set problem?
Can I pick the right diagram?
